analysis.one_liner: Wipes out existing hospital medical debt with federal money and bans collecting or credit-reporting it.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 2024 with two cosponsors, the bill died in the Senate health committee without a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a federal grant program that pays hospitals to cancel medical debt their patients owe, prioritizing safety-net hospitals and debts of low-income patients from emergency and non-elective care. It would bar collectors and creditors from pursuing any medical debt that existed before the law passed, stop medical debt from appearing on credit reports, and impose new billing rules: hospitals would have to screen patients for charity care before a bill is due, cap what uninsured patients at nonprofit hospitals can be charged, and stop charging interest on past-due medical bills.
analysis.who_benefits: People who carry medical debt would have it erased — the federal government would pay hospitals to cancel it, and older medical debt could no longer be collected or reported to credit bureaus. Patients going forward would get clearer bills, screening for charity care, and no interest charges on past-due medical balances.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes competitive federal grants to hospitals to eliminate eligible medical debt owed by patients, prioritizing safety-net hospitals and debts of low-income and vulnerable patients from emergency and non-elective care, with the program expanding after two years to other providers and individuals. [S2]
Prohibits any debt collector or creditor from collecting medical debt incurred before enactment, and gives consumers a private right to sue for damages and attorney's fees if they try. [S2]

Adds medical debt to the information credit reporting agencies are barred from including in consumer reports, 30 days after enactment, and requires agencies to notify consumers when they remove it. [S2]

Requires providers to screen patients for charity care eligibility at least 45 days before payment is due, publish a federal list of financial-assistance programs, cap charges to uninsured patients at nonprofit hospitals at the amounts generally billed, prohibit interest on past-due medical payments, and hold outside collection contractors to the same rules. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund the grant program that pays hospitals for the debt being canceled. Hospitals would give up interest income and some collection leverage, and face new billing and charity-care screening duties. Debt collectors and credit reporting agencies would lose medical debt as a business line.

drawbacks.text: The grant program would pay hospitals the full outstanding amount they claim patients owe, rather than buying that debt at the steep discounts it typically trades for on the secondary market, so each dollar of relief for a patient could cost taxpayers several dollars. [S2]

The bill cancels debt incurred before enactment but does not stop hospitals from generating new medical debt going forward; its billing and charity-care rules soften but do not eliminate future debt accumulation. [S2]

Eligible debt excludes anything already payable by federal health programs and amounts above what insurers or federal programs reimburse, so some of the debt patients experience would fall outside the program. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people carrying medical debt, the bill offers substantial, concrete relief: erased balances, no collection calls on old debt, and clean credit reports. The main cost is to taxpayers, and the design is inefficient — compensating hospitals at face value for debt that normally sells for pennies on the dollar makes relief far more expensive than it needs to be. The bill also leaves the underlying drivers of new medical debt mostly untouched, offering billing-rule fixes rather than a systemic solution.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice in the Senate and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, and no committee or floor action ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the Medical Debt Cancellation Act on May 8, 2024, joined by Senator Jeff Merkley as a co-introducer. [S1] [S2]
On the day of introduction, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions. [S4]
The bill attracted two cosponsors, both Senate Democrats. [S3]
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote followed; the recorded action history ends with the committee referral, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025. [S4] [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals keep their existing medical debt and their ability to collect it; debt collectors and credit reporting agencies keep medical debt as a business line. Americans with medical debt continue to owe it, and it can still be collected and reported.

sides.party_line_note: Support came only from the Independent sponsor and two Senate Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never reached a vote where positions could be recorded.

industries.note: Under the bill, hospitals would be paid by federal grants to cancel debt patients owe them — turning uncollected receivables into federal money — while also facing new charity-care screening duties, a cap on charges to uninsured patients, and a ban on interest on past-due bills. The grant side pays them; the billing rules trim their collection practices.

The bill makes all pre-enactment medical debt uncollectible and exposes collectors to lawsuits with damages and attorney's fees, wiping out medical debt as a collection business line. Their interest in pursuing these balances runs directly against debtors' interest in being left alone.

The bill bars credit bureaus from including medical debt in consumer reports and requires them to strip existing entries, removing data they currently sell and a mechanism that lowers borrowers' credit scores. Their interest in reporting this debt runs against people trying to keep their credit intact.
